Thai Fisheries Firm Siam Marine Harvest Enters Liquidation Amid Market Headwinds

Siam Marine Harvest Co., a prominent player in Thailand’s fisheries sector, has entered liquidation after failing to overcome prolonged market challenges, the company confirmed on Wednesday. The development marks the most significant insolvency in the Thai fisheries industry in recent years, raising immediate concerns for ongoing operations, employment, and industry stability.

The Bangkok-based company, known for its export-oriented shrimp and tilapia production, filed for court-supervised liquidation on June 11. “We have made every effort to maintain business continuity in the face of unprecedented pressures, but unfortunately, the current environment left us with no viable alternatives,” said Chanin Rattanapong, Siam Marine Harvest’s Chief Executive Officer, in a statement. “Our priorities now are to ensure an orderly wind-down of operations and to treat our employees and stakeholders with transparency and fairness.”

According to documents submitted to the Central Bankruptcy Court, Siam Marine Harvest’s outstanding liabilities reached THB 1.8 billion (approximately USD 50 million), with significant debts owed to both domestic and international creditors. The company employs 470 staff across its processing plant in Samut Sakhon and aquaculture farms in Chachoengsao province. All production activities have ceased as of Tuesday, with only a skeletal staff retained to assist liquidators in asset management and administrative tasks.

The Federation of Thai Fisheries issued a statement expressing concern over the firm’s collapse. “Siam Marine Harvest has been a major contributor to export volumes and employment within the sector. Its liquidation will have a direct impact on the availability of farmed seafood for both domestic consumption and export,” said Prasert Jantapong, the Federation’s president. He added, “We urge the authorities to support affected workers and monitor the situation closely to safeguard the competitiveness of Thai fisheries.”

Industry analysts point to a confluence of factors behind the insolvency, including sustained low farm-gate prices, rising input costs, and persistent export market volatility. “The sector has faced mounting headwinds from fluctuating demand and disease outbreaks in farmed stock,” said Dr. Nattapol Srithep, a fisheries economist at the University of Chulalongkorn. “Siam Marine Harvest’s case demonstrates the urgent need for industry-wide reforms and improved risk management.”

At the time of writing, the company’s remaining inventory is being assessed and prepared for sale to satisfy creditor claims. Meetings with employees and creditors are ongoing, with further announcements expected from the liquidators in the coming days. The wider fisheries industry is monitoring the situation, with stakeholders concerned about potential ripple effects on supply and sector confidence.
